title: The nightly drive from New Jersey and never being late
summary: Playing from ten to four needed no warm-up; he drove forty-two miles up the Hudson nightly and missed only one night, in a snowstorm.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: You used to play from ten to four - now, what time would you get there? Most of the time you were at Conden's you were living out in the country--

Well, you see, in those days, I really didn't have to warm up because I played so much. So many hours. I'd just come in --- I'd get there half hour - three-quarters of an hour ahead of time - I'd go down to the basement blow a few toots and I didn't have to do like I have to do now. I have to practice now, to get my lip softened up. But, when you play those kind of hours, my God, you don't need to practice - you know.
After you got through playing, you'd drive back out in the country and, then, this went on
for most of the time you were at Conden's--
Well, about twelve years of the time I was living out--- I lived in New Jersey, you know.
And, then, that was a drive too. Over the George Washington Bridge and the way I'd go -- 42 miles up the Hudson.
And, I used to do that-- I did that every night and I never was late once in my whole career in that club.
I'm not sure you've ever been late anywhere - have you?
The only time I missed the whole performance was the time I couldn't get out of the snow where I lived.
I couldn't get up the hill; I just couldn't get out.
